ncert_questions.q: Mention the advantages of selecting pea plant for experiment by Mendel.
ncert_questions.a: Mendel chose garden pea (Pisum sativum) because: (i) it has many easily distinguishable, contrasting characters (tall/dwarf, round/wrinkled seeds, and so on) that are inherited without intermediates; (ii) its flowers are bisexual and normally self-pollinating, so true-breeding lines are easily maintained, while cross-pollination can be carried out by hand after emasculation; (iii) it has a short life cycle and produces a large number of seeds in one generation, giving large samples for statistical analysis; (iv) it is an annual, easy to grow and needs little space.

ncert_questions.q: Differentiate between the following: (a) Dominance and Recessive (b) Homozygous and Heterozygous (c) Monohybrid and Dihybrid.
ncert_questions.a:
(a) A dominant allele expresses itself in both the homozygous and the heterozygous condition and produces a functional product (T). A recessive allele is masked in the heterozygote and expresses only in the homozygous condition; it produces a non-functional product or no product (t).

(b) A homozygous individual carries two identical alleles of a gene (TT or tt), produces only one kind of gamete for that gene and breeds true. A heterozygous individual carries two different alleles (Tt), produces two kinds of gametes and does not breed true.

(c) A monohybrid cross involves parents differing in one character (TT × tt) and gives a 3 : 1 F2 ratio; a dihybrid cross involves parents differing in two characters (RRYY × rryy) and gives a 9 : 3 : 3 : 1 F2 ratio.

ncert_questions.q: A diploid organism is heterozygous for 4 loci, how many types of gametes can be produced?
ncert_questions.a: An organism heterozygous at n loci produces 2n types of gametes, because each locus contributes either of its two alleles independently. For 4 loci (AaBbCcDd), the number of gamete types is 24 = 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 = 16.

ncert_questions.q: Explain the Law of Dominance using a monohybrid cross.
ncert_questions.a:
The law of dominance states that (i) characters are controlled by discrete units called factors, (ii) factors occur in pairs, and (iii) in a dissimilar pair of factors one member dominates (dominant) the other (recessive).

Monohybrid cross: true-breeding tall (TT) × true-breeding dwarf (tt). Gametes T and t. F1 all Tt, and all are tall, showing that T is dominant over t: the dwarf trait is present but masked. On selfing the F1, gametes T and t from each parent combine in a Punnett square to give TT, Tt, Tt, tt, that is 3 tall : 1 dwarf. The dwarf character reappears unchanged in the F2, proving it was only masked in F1, not lost or blended. The law explains the expression of only one parental character in F1 and of both in F2 in the proportion 3 : 1.

ncert_questions.q: Define and design a test cross.
ncert_questions.a:
A test cross is a cross between an individual showing the dominant phenotype (of unknown genotype) and its homozygous recessive parent, done to find whether the individual is homozygous or heterozygous.

Design: take a violet-flowered pea plant (VV or Vv) and cross it with a white-flowered plant (vv).

  • If the plant is VV: VV × vv → gametes V and v → all progeny Vv, all violet. No white progeny, so the parent is homozygous.
  • If the plant is Vv: Vv × vv → gametes V, v and v → 1 Vv : 1 vv, that is 1 violet : 1 white. The appearance of white progeny (50 per cent) shows the parent is heterozygous.

The 1 : 1 ratio also demonstrates the law of segregation.

ncert_questions.q: Using a Punnett Square, work out the distribution of phenotypic features in the first filial generation after a cross between a homozygous female and a heterozygous male for a single locus.
ncert_questions.a:
Take height in pea, T dominant over t. Two cases arise.

Case 1: homozygous dominant female TT × heterozygous male Tt. Female gametes T only; male gametes T and t. Punnett square: TT, Tt. Genotypes 1 TT : 1 Tt; phenotype: all tall (100 per cent).

Case 2: homozygous recessive female tt × heterozygous male Tt. Female gametes t; male gametes T and t. Punnett square: Tt, tt. Genotypes 1 Tt : 1 tt; phenotype 1 tall : 1 dwarf (50 per cent each). This second cross is a test cross.

ncert_questions.q: When a cross is made between a tall plant with yellow seeds (TtYy) and a tall plant with green seeds (Ttyy), what proportions of phenotype in the offspring could be expected to be (a) tall and green, (b) dwarf and green?
ncert_questions.a:
Treat the two genes separately since they assort independently.

Height: Tt × Tt → TT, Tt, Tt, tt → tall 3/4, dwarf 1/4.

Seed colour: Yy × yy → Yy, yy → yellow 1/2, green 1/2.

(a) Tall and green = 3/4 × 1/2 = 3/8 (that is 6 out of 16, or 37.5 per cent).

(b) Dwarf and green = 1/4 × 1/2 = 1/8 (2 out of 16, or 12.5 per cent).

Check: the four phenotypes are tall yellow 3/8, tall green 3/8, dwarf yellow 1/8, dwarf green 1/8, which sum to 1 (ratio 3 : 3 : 1 : 1). A 4 × 4 Punnett square with gametes TY, Ty, tY, ty against Ty and ty gives the same counts.

ncert_questions.q: Two heterozygous parents are crossed. If the two loci are linked what would be the distribution of phenotypic features in F<sub>1</sub> generation for a dihybrid cross?
ncert_questions.a: Linked genes lie on the same chromosome and are inherited together; they do not assort independently. So the cross of two double heterozygotes (say AB/ab × AB/ab, both alleles in the coupling phase) does not give the 9 : 3 : 3 : 1 ratio expected for independent genes. Each parent produces mainly the parental gametes AB and ab, with very few recombinant gametes Ab and aB (formed only by crossing over between the two loci). The progeny therefore show predominantly the parental phenotypes, and with complete linkage the two genes behave as one unit giving 3 (both dominant) : 1 (both recessive). The proportion of recombinant phenotypes depends on the distance between the two loci: tightly linked genes give almost none, loosely linked genes give more, as Morgan found in Drosophila (1.3 per cent for yellow body and white eye, 37.2 per cent for white eye and miniature wing).

ncert_questions.q: Briefly mention the contribution of T. H. Morgan in genetics.
ncert_questions.a: Thomas Hunt Morgan worked on the fruit fly Drosophila melanogaster and (i) provided the experimental verification of the chromosomal theory of inheritance proposed by Sutton and Boveri; (ii) discovered sex-linked inheritance through the white-eye gene on the X chromosome; (iii) discovered linkage: genes located on the same chromosome are physically associated and inherited together, so they do not follow independent assortment; (iv) explained recombination as the generation of non-parental combinations by crossing over, and showed that its frequency depends on the distance between genes (98.7 per cent parental types for yellow body and white eye, 62.8 per cent for white eye and miniature wing). His student Sturtevant used these recombination frequencies to construct the first genetic maps.

ncert_questions.q: What is pedigree analysis? Suggest how such an analysis can be useful.
ncert_questions.a:
Pedigree analysis is the study of the inheritance of a particular trait through several generations of a family, represented as a family tree with standard symbols (square for male, circle for female, shaded symbols for affected individuals, horizontal mating lines, generations numbered I, II, III).

Uses: (i) it tells whether a trait is dominant or recessive, and autosomal or sex-linked, from its pattern of appearance; (ii) it traces hereditary diseases such as haemophilia, colour blindness, sickle cell anaemia and thalassaemia through a family; (iii) it identifies carriers and predicts the probability of a couple having an affected child, which is the basis of genetic counselling; (iv) it is the only way to study inheritance in humans, where controlled crosses cannot be made.

ncert_questions.q: How is sex determined in human beings?
ncert_questions.a: Humans have 23 pairs of chromosomes: 22 pairs of autosomes and one pair of sex chromosomes. Females have two X chromosomes (XX); males have one X and one Y (XY). The female produces only one kind of ovum, 22A + X. The male produces two kinds of sperm in equal numbers, 22A + X and 22A + Y (male heterogamety). If an X-bearing sperm fertilises the ovum, the zygote is XX and develops into a female; if a Y-bearing sperm fertilises it, the zygote is XY and develops into a male. So the sex of the child is determined by the sperm, that is by the father, and the chance of a boy or a girl at each conception is 1 : 1.

ncert_questions.q: A child has blood group O. If the father has blood group A and mother blood group B, work out the genotypes of the parents and the possible genotypes of the other offspring.
ncert_questions.a:
Blood group O has genotype ii, so the child received one i allele from each parent. A father with group A who carries i must be IAi; a mother with group B who carries i must be IBi.

Cross IAi × IBi. Father's gametes IA, i; mother's gametes IB, i. Punnett square gives IAIB (group AB), IAi (group A), IBi (group B) and ii (group O), each with probability 1/4. So the other offspring can have any of the four blood groups, in the ratio 1 AB : 1 A : 1 B : 1 O.

ncert_questions.q: Explain the following terms with example: (a) Co-dominance (b) Incomplete dominance.
ncert_questions.a:
(a) Co-dominance: both alleles of a gene express themselves fully in the heterozygote, so the F1 resembles both parents and no intermediate forms. Example: ABO blood groups. Alleles IA and IB each produce their own sugar on the RBC surface; a person with IAIB has both A and B antigens and belongs to group AB.

(b) Incomplete dominance: neither allele is completely dominant, so the heterozygote shows an intermediate phenotype. Example: flower colour in snapdragon (Antirrhinum). Red (RR) × white (rr) gives pink (Rr) F1; the F2 on selfing is 1 red : 2 pink : 1 white, so the phenotypic ratio equals the genotypic ratio 1 : 2 : 1.

ncert_questions.q: What is point mutation? Give one example.
ncert_questions.a: A point mutation is a mutation arising from a change (substitution) in a single base pair of DNA. Example: sickle cell anaemia, in which the sixth codon of the β-globin gene changes from GAG to GUG (in mRNA), so glutamic acid is replaced by valine at the sixth position of the β-globin chain of haemoglobin. The abnormal haemoglobin HbS polymerises under low oxygen tension and the RBC becomes sickle-shaped.

ncert_questions.q: Who had proposed the chromosomal theory of inheritance?
ncert_questions.a: Walter Sutton and Theodore Boveri (1902). They noted the parallel between the behaviour of chromosomes during meiosis and the behaviour of Mendel's factors, and proposed that genes are located on chromosomes, which segregate and assort independently. Thomas Hunt Morgan later verified it experimentally in Drosophila.

ncert_questions.q: Mention any two autosomal genetic disorders with their symptoms.
ncert_questions.a: (i) Sickle cell anaemia (autosomal recessive): substitution of glutamic acid by valine at the sixth position of the β-globin chain; RBCs become sickle-shaped under low oxygen tension, leading to anaemia, blocked capillaries and organ damage. (ii) Phenylketonuria (autosomal recessive): lack of phenylalanine hydroxylase; phenylalanine accumulates and is converted to phenylpyruvic acid, which causes mental retardation and is excreted in urine; hair and skin pigmentation is reduced. (Also acceptable: thalassaemia, autosomal recessive, reduced synthesis of α or β globin chain causing anaemia; Down's syndrome is an autosomal chromosomal disorder, trisomy 21, with short stature, furrowed tongue, broad palm crease and retarded mental development.)

pyq.q: A test cross is carried out to
options: determine the genotype of a plant showing the dominant phenotype
determine the phenotype of a plant
assess the number of alleles of a gene
predict whether two genes are linked
pyq.answer: a
pyq.solution: A test cross with the homozygous recessive parent reveals whether a dominant-phenotype individual is TT (all dominant progeny) or Tt (1 : 1 progeny).

pyq.q: The number of different kinds of gametes produced by an organism with the genotype AaBbCcDd is
pyq.answer: c
pyq.solution: Four heterozygous loci give 2<sup>4</sup> = 16 gamete types (NCERT exercise 4.3).

pyq.q: In snapdragon, a cross between a red-flowered plant and a white-flowered plant gave all pink-flowered F<sub>1</sub>. The F<sub>2</sub> obtained by selfing the F<sub>1</sub> will show the phenotypic ratio
pyq.answer: b
pyq.solution: Incomplete dominance: RR red, Rr pink, rr white, so the F<sub>2</sub> phenotypic ratio equals the genotypic ratio 1 : 2 : 1.

pyq.q: A woman with blood group AB marries a man with blood group O. The blood groups possible in their children are
pyq.answer: b
pyq.solution: I<sup>A</sup>I<sup>B</sup> × ii gives I<sup>A</sup>i (group A) and I<sup>B</sup>i (group B) only, each 50 per cent.

pyq.q: In Morgan's experiments on Drosophila, which pair of genes showed the highest recombination frequency?
pyq.answer: b
pyq.solution: White eye and miniature wing gave 37.2 per cent recombinants (62.8 per cent parental) against 1.3 per cent for yellow body and white eye, so they are more loosely linked.

pyq.q: Female heterogamety is found in
pyq.answer: d
pyq.solution: In birds the female is ZW and produces two kinds of eggs (Z and W); humans, Drosophila (XY) and grasshopper (XO) show male heterogamety.

pyq.q: A drone (male honey bee) has
options: 32 chromosomes and develops from a fertilised egg
16 chromosomes and develops from an unfertilised egg
16 chromosomes and develops from a fertilised egg
32 chromosomes and develops from an unfertilised egg
pyq.answer: b
pyq.solution: Honey bee is haplodiploid: unfertilised eggs develop parthenogenetically into haploid (n = 16) males; fertilised eggs give diploid (32) females.

pyq.q: Which of the following is a correct match?
pyq.answer: c
pyq.solution: Down's syndrome is trisomy 21 (47 chromosomes). Klinefelter's is XXY, Turner's is XO, and phenylketonuria is autosomal recessive.

pyq.q: In sickle cell anaemia, the amino acid substitution in the β-globin chain is
options: valine replaced by glutamic acid at position 6
glutamic acid replaced by valine at position 6
glutamic acid replaced by lysine at position 6
valine replaced by glutamic acid at position 1
pyq.answer: b
pyq.solution: A point mutation GAG → GUG in the sixth codon replaces glutamic acid with valine at the sixth position of the β-globin chain.

pyq.q: Assertion (A): In humans the sex of the child is determined by the father. Reason (R): The human male is heterogametic and produces two types of sperm, one with X and one with Y chromosome, while the female produces only X-bearing ova.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
pyq.answer: a
pyq.solution: Whether the zygote is XX or XY depends only on which sperm fertilises the ovum, so the male gamete decides the sex.

pyq.q: Assertion (A): A haemophilic father cannot transmit haemophilia to his son. Reason (R): Haemophilia is an X-linked recessive disorder and a son receives his X chromosome from his mother.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
pyq.answer: a
pyq.solution: The father gives his Y chromosome to sons and his X (with the haemophilia allele) only to daughters, who become carriers.

pyq.q: Assertion (A): Genes for yellow body and white eye in Drosophila show very little recombination. Reason (R): The two genes are located far apart on the X chromosome.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
pyq.answer: c
pyq.solution: The genes showed only 1.3 per cent recombination because they are tightly linked, that is very close together on the X chromosome; R states the opposite.

pyq.q: Assertion (A): Down's syndrome is an example of polyploidy. Reason (R): Down's syndrome results from the presence of an extra copy of chromosome 21.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
pyq.answer: d
pyq.solution: An extra single chromosome is aneuploidy (trisomy), not polyploidy, which is an increase in a whole set of chromosomes. R is a correct statement.

pyq.q: Why did Morgan choose Drosophila melanogaster for his genetic experiments? Give any four reasons.
pyq.answer: (i) It can be grown on a simple synthetic medium in the laboratory. (ii) It completes its life cycle in about two weeks. (iii) A single mating produces a large number of progeny. (iv) It shows clear sexual dimorphism, so males and females are easily distinguished. (v) It has many types of hereditary variations that can be seen with a low-power microscope. Any four earn full marks.

pyq.q: Differentiate between co-dominance and incomplete dominance with one example of each.
pyq.answer: Incomplete dominance: neither allele is completely dominant, so the heterozygote shows an intermediate phenotype that resembles neither parent; example, pink flowers of Rr snapdragon from red RR × white rr. Co-dominance: both alleles express themselves fully and independently in the heterozygote, which resembles both parents; example, blood group AB in IAIB individuals, who have both A and B antigens. In both cases the F2 phenotypic ratio is 1 : 2 : 1.

pyq.q: Differentiate between multiple allelism and pleiotropy with one example each.
pyq.answer: Multiple allelism: a single gene exists in more than two allelic forms in a population, although an individual carries only two; example, the ABO blood group gene I with alleles IA, IB and i. Pleiotropy: a single gene controls more than one phenotypic character; example, the phenylketonuria gene, whose mutation causes mental retardation and reduced hair and skin pigmentation (or the pea starch-synthesis gene controlling seed shape and starch grain size).

pyq.q: Distinguish between male heterogamety and female heterogamety with an example of each.
pyq.answer: Male heterogamety: the male produces two different kinds of gametes with respect to the sex chromosome, and the female only one kind; examples, humans and Drosophila (XY male producing X- and Y-sperm) and grasshopper (XO male producing X- and no-X sperm). Female heterogamety: the female produces two kinds of gametes and the male one kind; example, birds, where the female is ZW (Z and W eggs) and the male ZZ (only Z sperm).

pyq.q: How is aneuploidy different from polyploidy? Give one example of each.
pyq.answer: Aneuploidy is the gain or loss of one or more individual chromosomes, caused by failure of segregation of chromatids (non-disjunction) during cell division; example, Down's syndrome (trisomy 21) or Turner's syndrome (XO). Polyploidy is an increase in a whole set of chromosomes (3n, 4n), caused by failure of cytokinesis after telophase; it is often observed in plants, for example triploid banana or tetraploid wheat, and is rare in animals.

pyq.q: A haemophilic father can never pass the gene for haemophilia to his son. Explain.
pyq.answer: Haemophilia is X-linked recessive; the gene lies on the X chromosome. A son receives his Y chromosome from the father and his X chromosome from the mother. Since the father contributes only Y to a son, the haemophilia allele on the father's X can never reach his son. The father passes the Xh chromosome to all his daughters, who become carriers (XHXh); the disease reaches a grandson through such a carrier daughter.

pyq.q: Mendel published his work in 1865, but it remained unrecognised till 1900. Give three reasons for the delay in acceptance of his work, and name the scientists who rediscovered it.
pyq.answer: (i) Communication was not easy in those days, so his work could not be widely publicised. (ii) His concept of genes (factors) as stable and discrete units that control the expression of traits, and of the pair of alleles that did not 'blend' with each other, was not accepted by his contemporaries as an explanation for the apparently continuous variation seen in nature. (iii) His approach of using mathematics to explain biological phenomena was totally new and unacceptable to many biologists of the time. (iv) He could not provide any physical proof for the existence of factors or say what they were made of. In 1900 three scientists, de Vries, Correns and von Tschermak, independently rediscovered Mendel's results, by which time chromosomes had been observed and their behaviour in cell division was known.

pyq.q: A red-flowered snapdragon plant is crossed with a white-flowered one. Work out the cross up to the F<sub>2</sub> generation, giving the phenotypic and genotypic ratios. Name the phenomenon.
pyq.answer:
Parents: red RR × white rr. Gametes: R and r. F1: all Rr, pink flowers (neither parent's colour, so R is incompletely dominant over r).

F1 × F1: Rr × Rr; gametes R and r from each. Punnett square: RR (red), Rr (pink), Rr (pink), rr (white).

F2 genotypic ratio 1 RR : 2 Rr : 1 rr; phenotypic ratio 1 red : 2 pink : 1 white. The two ratios are identical because each genotype has its own phenotype. The phenomenon is incomplete dominance: the heterozygote shows an intermediate phenotype since one dose of R makes less pigment than two.

pyq.q: Explain the experiments of Morgan on linkage in Drosophila. What did he conclude about the relationship between linkage strength and distance between genes?
pyq.answer:
Morgan carried out dihybrid crosses in Drosophila using pairs of sex-linked genes on the X chromosome. He crossed yellow-bodied, white-eyed females with brown-bodied, red-eyed males, and in a second cross white-eyed, miniature-winged flies with red-eyed, normal-winged flies, and studied the F2. He found that the two genes did not segregate independently of each other: parental combinations were far more frequent than the non-parental (recombinant) combinations expected from a 9 : 3 : 3 : 1 ratio. For yellow body and white eye the F2 had 98.7 per cent parental and 1.3 per cent recombinant types; for white eye and miniature wing, 62.8 per cent parental and 37.2 per cent recombinant.

He attributed this to the physical association or linkage of genes on the same chromosome, and called the generation of non-parental combinations recombination. He concluded that genes close together on a chromosome are tightly linked and show low recombination, while genes far apart are loosely linked and show high recombination; that is, linkage strength is inversely proportional and recombination frequency directly proportional to the distance between the genes. Sturtevant used this to map genes.

pyq.q: Explain polygenic inheritance with the help of the example of human skin colour.
pyq.answer: A polygenic trait is one controlled by three or more genes, in which each dominant allele contributes an additive, equal effect to the phenotype and the environment also has an influence. Such traits show a continuous gradation rather than discrete classes. Human skin colour is controlled by (say) three genes A, B and C. Dominant alleles A, B and C add pigment; recessive alleles a, b and c do not. AABBCC (six dominant alleles) is the darkest, aabbcc (none) is the lightest, and AaBbCc (three) has an intermediate colour. The phenotype depends only on the number of dominant alleles, so AABbcc, AaBBcc and aaBbCC are all equally intermediate. Selfing AaBbCc gives seven classes from 0 to 6 dominant alleles in the proportion 1 : 6 : 15 : 20 : 15 : 6 : 1, a bell-shaped distribution. Human height is inherited the same way.

pyq.q: Describe the mechanism of sex determination in honey bee. Why is a drone said to have no father but a grandfather?
pyq.answer:
Honey bee shows the haplodiploid sex-determination system. Sex depends on the number of sets of chromosomes, not on sex chromosomes. An egg fertilised by a sperm develops into a diploid female (queen or worker) with 32 chromosomes. An unfertilised egg develops by parthenogenesis into a haploid male (drone) with 16 chromosomes. Since the drone is haploid, it produces sperm by mitosis, and all its sperm are identical.

A drone develops from an unfertilised egg, so no sperm contributed to it: it has no father. But its mother, the queen, developed from a fertilised egg and had a father, so the drone has a grandfather. Likewise a drone cannot have sons (its sperm fertilise eggs which become daughters) but its daughters can lay unfertilised eggs, so it can have grandsons.

pyq.q: Prepare a table showing the chromosomal constitution, sex of the affected individual and two symptoms of Down's syndrome, Klinefelter's syndrome and Turner's syndrome.
pyq.answer:
Down's syndrome: 45A + XX or 45A + XY (47 chromosomes), trisomy of chromosome 21; occurs in both sexes; short stature, small round head, furrowed tongue, partially open mouth, broad palm with characteristic crease, retarded physical, psychomotor and mental development.

Klinefelter's syndrome: 44A + XXY (47 chromosomes), an extra X chromosome; phenotypic male; overall masculine development with feminine features such as breast development (gynaecomastia); sterile.

Turner's syndrome: 44A + XO (45 chromosomes), one X chromosome missing; phenotypic female; rudimentary ovaries, lack of other secondary sexual characters; sterile.

All three are aneuploidies arising from non-disjunction of chromosomes during gamete formation.

pyq.q: A pea plant homozygous for round yellow seeds is crossed with one having wrinkled green seeds. Work out the cross up to the F<sub>2</sub> generation using a Punnett square and state the law that this cross illustrates.
pyq.answer:
Round (R) is dominant over wrinkled (r); yellow (Y) is dominant over green (y).

Parents: RRYY (round yellow) × rryy (wrinkled green). Gametes: RY and ry. F1: RrYy, all round yellow.

F1 selfed: RrYy × RrYy. Each produces four kinds of gametes, RY, Ry, rY, ry, in equal numbers, because the alleles of the two genes assort independently. Placing these on both sides of a 4 × 4 Punnett square gives 16 combinations:

Row RY: RRYY, RRYy, RrYY, RrYy · Row Ry: RRYy, RRyy, RrYy, Rryy · Row rY: RrYY, RrYy, rrYY, rrYy · Row ry: RrYy, Rryy, rrYy, rryy.

Phenotypes: round yellow (R_Y_) 9, round green (R_yy) 3, wrinkled yellow (rrY_) 3, wrinkled green (rryy) 1. F2 phenotypic ratio 9 : 3 : 3 : 1 (Mendel counted 315 : 108 : 101 : 32). Genotypic ratio 1 : 2 : 2 : 4 : 1 : 2 : 1 : 2 : 1. Taking one character at a time, round : wrinkled = 12 : 4 = 3 : 1 and yellow : green = 3 : 1, so each gene segregates as in a monohybrid cross.

The cross illustrates Mendel's Law of Independent Assortment: when two pairs of traits are combined in a hybrid, segregation of one pair of characters is independent of the other pair of characters. The physical basis is the independent orientation of different homologous pairs at metaphase I of meiosis.

pyq.q: (a) State the chromosomal theory of inheritance and name the scientists who proposed it. (b) Explain the parallel behaviour of chromosomes and Mendel's factors that led to the theory. (c) Who provided its experimental verification and in which organism?
pyq.answer:
(a) The chromosomal theory of inheritance, proposed by Walter Sutton and Theodore Boveri in 1902, states that genes (Mendel's factors) are located on chromosomes, and that it is the chromosomes that segregate and assort independently during meiosis, so the behaviour of chromosomes accounts for Mendel's laws.

(b) Sutton and Boveri united the knowledge of chromosomal segregation with Mendelian principles by noticing these parallels: (i) chromosomes occur in pairs, and so do the factors; (ii) one member of each chromosome pair comes from each parent, and one allele of each gene pair comes from each parent; (iii) homologous chromosomes separate during meiosis so that each gamete receives one of each pair, which is the law of segregation of alleles; (iv) different chromosome pairs separate independently of one another at anaphase I, which is the law of independent assortment of different genes; (v) both alleles of a gene occupy the same position (locus) on the two homologous chromosomes. Chromosomes are thus the physical carriers of the factors.

(c) Thomas Hunt Morgan and his colleagues verified the theory experimentally in the fruit fly Drosophila melanogaster, chosen because it grows on a simple synthetic medium, completes its life cycle in about two weeks, gives many progeny per mating, shows sexual dimorphism, and has many visible hereditary variations. Their dihybrid crosses with X-linked genes showed that genes on the same chromosome are linked and do not assort independently, confirming that genes lie on chromosomes.

pyq.q: Describe the mechanism of sex determination in (a) grasshopper, (b) humans and (c) birds. Which of these show male heterogamety and which show female heterogamety?
pyq.answer:
(a) Grasshopper (XX–XO type): the female has two X chromosomes (XX) and the male only one (XO), so the male has one chromosome fewer. All eggs carry an X. The male produces two kinds of sperm in equal numbers, with an X and without an X. An egg fertilised by an X-sperm becomes XX (female); one fertilised by a sperm lacking X becomes XO (male). Henking (1891) first observed this 'X body' in insect spermatogenesis.

(b) Humans (XX–XY type): both sexes have 46 chromosomes, 22 pairs of autosomes and one pair of sex chromosomes. The female is XX and the male XY, the Y being smaller. The female produces one kind of ovum (22A + X); the male produces two kinds of sperm, 22A + X and 22A + Y, in equal numbers. Fertilisation by an X-sperm gives XX (female); by a Y-sperm gives XY (male). The sex of the child is therefore decided by the father's sperm, with a 50 : 50 chance each time. Drosophila has the same system.

(c) Birds (ZW–ZZ type): the female has two dissimilar sex chromosomes (ZW) and the male two similar ones (ZZ). The female produces two kinds of eggs, with Z or with W; the male produces only Z-sperm. An egg with Z fertilised by Z-sperm becomes ZZ (male); an egg with W becomes ZW (female).

Grasshopper and humans show male heterogamety (the male makes two kinds of gametes); birds show female heterogamety (the female makes two kinds of gametes). Honey bee, by contrast, uses haplodiploidy with no heterogametic sex at all.

pyq.q: (a) Compare sickle cell anaemia and thalassaemia with respect to their inheritance, the molecular defect and the nature of the defect. (b) Explain, with a cross, why two apparently normal parents can have a child with sickle cell anaemia.
pyq.answer:
(a) Both are autosomal recessive Mendelian disorders of haemoglobin, transmitted from unaffected carrier parents to some of their offspring, and both affect males and females equally. Sickle cell anaemia is controlled by a single pair of alleles HbA and HbS. The defect is a point mutation, GAG → GUG, in the sixth codon of the β-globin gene, replacing glutamic acid with valine at the sixth position of the β-globin chain. The mutant haemoglobin polymerises under low oxygen tension and changes the biconcave RBC into a sickle shape. The defect is qualitative: the globin is made in normal amount but functions incorrectly. Thalassaemia is caused by mutation or deletion that reduces the rate of synthesis of a globin chain. α-thalassaemia involves the two closely linked genes HBA1 and HBA2 on chromosome 16 (the more of the four genes affected, the less α-globin made); β-thalassaemia involves one or both HBB genes on chromosome 11. The defect is quantitative: too few globin molecules, giving abnormal haemoglobin and anaemia.

(b) Two apparently normal parents can both be heterozygous carriers, HbAHbS. The disease is recessive, so carriers have enough normal haemoglobin to be unaffected. Cross: HbAHbS × HbAHbS; gametes HbA and HbS from each parent. Punnett square: HbAHbA (normal), HbAHbS (carrier), HbAHbS (carrier), HbSHbS (diseased). So at each conception there is a 1 in 4 (25 per cent) chance of an affected child, a 1 in 2 chance of a carrier and a 1 in 4 chance of a fully normal child.

pyq.q:
Read the passage and answer the questions. A pedigree of a family is studied for haemophilia. In generation I, a normal man marries a woman whose father was haemophilic. In generation II they have two sons and two daughters; one son is haemophilic, the other is normal, and both daughters are normal. One daughter later marries a normal man and in generation III has a haemophilic son.
(i) State the type of inheritance shown by haemophilia and give one observation from the pedigree that supports it.
(ii) Write the genotype of the woman in generation I and explain how you know it.
(iii) What is the probability that the next son of the generation II daughter will be haemophilic?
(iv) Can a daughter of the haemophilic son in generation II be haemophilic if he marries a normal non-carrier woman? Give a reason.
pyq.answer:
(i) X-linked (sex-linked) recessive. Only males are affected while the females who transmit it are unaffected, and the trait skips a generation by passing from a carrier mother to her son.

(ii) XHXh, a carrier. Her father was haemophilic (XhY), so she must have received his Xh; she is unaffected, so her other X is XH. Her haemophilic son confirms it, since a son's X comes only from the mother.

(iii) The generation II daughter has a haemophilic son, so she is a carrier XHXh. Her cross with a normal man XHY gives sons XHY and XhY in equal proportion, so the probability that a son is haemophilic is 1/2 (50 per cent).

(iv) No. The haemophilic son (XhY) gives his Xh to every daughter, but a non-carrier mother gives XH, so all daughters are XHXh, unaffected carriers. A haemophilic daughter would require a haemophilic father and at least a carrier mother.

pyq.q:
Read the passage and answer the questions. Morgan crossed Drosophila flies in two separate dihybrid experiments using genes located on the X chromosome. In experiment A (yellow body and white eye) the F2 showed 98.7 per cent parental combinations and 1.3 per cent recombinants. In experiment B (white eye and miniature wing) the F2 showed 62.8 per cent parental combinations and 37.2 per cent recombinants.
(i) Why did neither experiment give the 9 : 3 : 3 : 1 ratio expected from Mendel's dihybrid cross?
(ii) Which pair of genes is more tightly linked? Justify.
(iii) Define recombination and name the process at meiosis that produces the recombinant types.
(iv) How did Sturtevant use such data, and what later use did his work find?
pyq.answer:
(i) The two genes in each experiment are on the same chromosome (the X), so they are linked and inherited together instead of assorting independently. Independent assortment, and hence 9 : 3 : 3 : 1, applies only to genes on different chromosomes.

(ii) Yellow body and white eye (experiment A). They gave only 1.3 per cent recombinants against 37.2 per cent for white eye and miniature wing, and the smaller the recombination frequency, the closer the genes lie and the stronger the linkage.

(iii) Recombination is the generation of non-parental gene combinations in the progeny. It is produced by crossing over, the exchange of segments between non-sister chromatids of homologous chromosomes during prophase I (pachytene) of meiosis.

(iv) Sturtevant used the frequency of recombination between gene pairs on the same chromosome as a measure of the distance between them and mapped their relative positions on the chromosome (genetic maps). Such maps were later used as a starting point in the sequencing of whole genomes in the Human Genome Project.

practice_mcq.q: Which of the following characters was NOT among the seven contrasting pairs studied by Mendel in garden pea?
practice_mcq.explanation: Mendel's seven characters were stem height, flower colour, flower position, pod shape, pod colour, seed shape and seed colour; leaf shape was not one of them.

practice_mcq.q: A tall pea plant on selfing produced 75 per cent tall and 25 per cent dwarf progeny. Its genotype is
practice_mcq.explanation: Only a heterozygote Tt gives the 3 : 1 ratio on selfing; TT would give all tall.

practice_mcq.q: The genotypic ratio of a monohybrid F<sub>2</sub> generation in a case of complete dominance is
practice_mcq.explanation: F<sub>2</sub> of Tt × Tt is 1 TT : 2 Tt : 1 tt; 3 : 1 is the phenotypic ratio.

practice_mcq.q: In a dihybrid test cross RrYy × rryy, the phenotypic ratio of the progeny is
practice_mcq.explanation: The recessive parent gives only ry gametes, so the progeny phenotypes reflect the four F<sub>1</sub> gamete types RY, Ry, rY, ry equally.

practice_mcq.q: Which of the following genotypes give blood group A?
practice_mcq.explanation: I<sup>A</sup> is dominant over i, so both I<sup>A</sup>I<sup>A</sup> and I<sup>A</sup>i express only the A antigen; I<sup>A</sup>I<sup>B</sup> is group AB.

practice_mcq.q: Starch grain size in pea seeds is an example of
practice_mcq.explanation: Bb seeds have starch grains of intermediate size between BB (large) and bb (small), so at this level B and b show incomplete dominance.

practice_mcq.q: The chromosomal theory of inheritance was proposed in 1902 by
options: de Vries, Correns and von Tschermak
practice_mcq.explanation: Sutton and Boveri linked chromosome behaviour at meiosis to Mendel's factors; the trio in option b rediscovered Mendel's work in 1900.

practice_mcq.q: The strength of linkage between two genes on a chromosome is
options: directly proportional to the distance between them
inversely proportional to the distance between them
independent of the distance between them
practice_mcq.explanation: The closer two genes lie, the fewer cross-overs occur between them, so linkage is stronger and recombination lower.

practice_mcq.q: Which of the following is the best example of a polygenic trait in humans?
practice_mcq.explanation: Skin colour is controlled by three or more genes with additive effects and shows continuous variation; the others are single-gene traits.

practice_mcq.q: A frameshift mutation is caused by
options: substitution of one base by another
insertion or deletion of one or two base pairs
practice_mcq.explanation: Insertions or deletions not in multiples of three shift the reading frame of the gene from that point onwards; a substitution is a point mutation.

practice_mcq.q: In a pedigree, two unaffected parents have an affected daughter. The trait is most likely
practice_mcq.explanation: Unaffected parents having an affected child shows the trait is recessive; an affected female with an unaffected father rules out X-linked recessive, since she would need an affected father.

practice_mcq.q: Phenylketonuria results from the absence of the enzyme
practice_mcq.explanation: Without phenylalanine hydroxylase, phenylalanine cannot be converted to tyrosine and accumulates as phenylpyruvic acid.

practice_mcq.q: Colour blindness affects about 8 per cent of males but only about 0.4 per cent of females because
options: the gene is on the Y chromosome
the gene is X-linked recessive and males have only one X
it is an autosomal dominant trait
females have a higher mutation rate
practice_mcq.explanation: A single recessive allele on the lone X of a male is expressed; a female needs two copies, which is far rarer.

practice_mcq.q: The genes for β-thalassaemia are located on chromosome
practice_mcq.explanation: β-thalassaemia involves the HBB gene on chromosome 11; α-thalassaemia involves HBA1 and HBA2 on chromosome 16.

practice_mcq.q: Gynaecomastia and sterility in a male with 47 chromosomes indicate
practice_mcq.explanation: Klinefelter's syndrome (XXY, 47 chromosomes) shows overall masculine development with breast development and sterility.

practice_mcq.q: Which statement about Turner's syndrome is correct?
options: It is caused by an extra X chromosome
It is caused by the absence of one X chromosome, giving 45 chromosomes
It is a trisomy of an autosome
practice_mcq.explanation: Turner's syndrome is 44A + XO with 45 chromosomes; the individual is a sterile female with rudimentary ovaries.

common_mistakes: Writing the F<sub>2</sub> ratio of a snapdragon cross as 3 : 1. In incomplete dominance the phenotypic ratio is 1 : 2 : 1, equal to the genotypic ratio; examiners deduct the ratio mark the moment 3 : 1 appears.

Drawing a cross without the gametes row or without the Punnett square. Marking schemes award separate marks for parents, gametes, the square and the ratio; a one-line answer gets one mark out of three or five.

Confusing multiple allelism with pleiotropy and with polygenic inheritance. Multiple alleles = many forms of one gene (ABO); pleiotropy = one gene, many effects (phenylketonuria); polygenic = many genes, one trait (skin colour).
Crediting Morgan with proposing the chromosomal theory. Sutton and Boveri proposed it (1902); Morgan verified it experimentally and discovered linkage.

Saying that genes far apart on a chromosome are tightly linked. Linkage strength falls with distance; recombination frequency rises with distance. Quote the 1.3 per cent and 37.2 per cent figures the right way round.
Writing ZZ for the female bird. In birds the female is ZW (heterogametic) and the male ZZ; it is the reverse of the human pattern.
Calling Down's syndrome polyploidy, or writing 46 chromosomes for it. An extra single chromosome is aneuploidy (trisomy 21), and the total is 47.

Giving haemophilia and colour blindness as autosomal, or sickle cell anaemia and thalassaemia as sex-linked. The first two are X-linked recessive; the others, along with phenylketonuria, are autosomal recessive.
Stating that the haemophilia carrier mother passes the disease to all her sons. Only half her sons are affected and half her daughters are carriers; show the cross.
Writing the sickle cell substitution as valine replaced by glutamic acid. It is glutamic acid replaced by valine at the sixth position of the β-globin chain, from GAG → GUG.
Forgetting that a drone is haploid and forms sperm by mitosis. 'Sperm by meiosis' in a honey bee answer is an error the examiner marks.
strategy:
Prepare this chapter in three passes. First, master the crosses, because they carry the 3- and 5-mark questions: monohybrid, test cross, dihybrid with the 16-box square, snapdragon, ABO blood-group crosses and the haemophilia carrier cross. Write each one out by hand with parents, gametes, Punnett square and both ratios until you can do it in under four minutes. The examiner does not accept a ratio without the square that produced it.

Second, memorise the facts that come as 1- and 2-mark items. Keep a single sheet with: Mendel's seven traits and his dates; the four reasons his work was ignored and the three rediscoverers; Sutton and Boveri, Morgan and Sturtevant with what each did; the two recombination percentages; the four sex-determination systems with the heterogametic sex and an example of each; the honey bee numbers 32 and 16; and for every disorder its inheritance type, chromosome or gene, molecular defect and two symptoms. Read that sheet twice a day for the last week.

Third, practise reading pedigrees and answering case studies: decide the type of inheritance from one observation, write genotypes, and calculate a probability. Pedigree, blood-group and Morgan-data case studies are the usual 4-mark passages from this chapter.

In the exam, give this chapter's 5-mark question about 12 minutes, most of it on a neat, fully labelled Punnett square. Use NCERT words: 'segregate', 'assort independently', 'heterogametic', 'non-disjunction', 'parthenogenesis'. Answer comparison questions in a two-column table. Do the NCERT exercises 3, 6, 7 and 12 from memory the night before; they are set almost verbatim.
